Your Mac isn’t “out of space.”

It’s holding $1,000+ of NVMe you already paid for, buried under agent caches, model shards, Docker leftovers, and 500 “temporary” worktrees.

Before you buy another 4TB drive: Storage Rescue Bot surveys read-only, shows what’s eating the disk. Only after you approve each group does it reclaim caches/build junk or offload big files to an external drive with SHA-256 verify-twice-then-delete. No “trust me, I deleted the right folder.”

Built for anyone running an AI agent fleet on a Mac... devs, content creators, etc. Or who's thinking about it.

What’s in the pack:
• Intake + ground rules. What must stay / agents in play.
• Read-only survey → classify A/B/C/D
• Question-widget approvals per group
• Offload protocol. Copy → remount re-verify → delete.
• External drive helpers
• Reclaim catalog. Official cleanups over blind `rm`.
• App-data + “System Data” playbooks

We ate our own dog food: ran it on my M5 128gb mbp when Data was ~99% full, cleared approved caches + Docker reclaimables + Trash and created  ~662 GiB of fresh new storage without touching models or live checkouts.

Ported, with gratitude, from @Da7_Tech's MIT-licensed Storage Rescue skill. Safety model and offload protocol are theirs; we reframed it for Grok Bot’s machine-targeted Shell + approval widgets.

note_tweet.text:
Most Reverse Engineer bots burn tokens decompiling everything first.

Reverse Lab does the opposite: 
1. Triage, one batched shell pass. `file`, strings, imports, caps. Label every claim SEEN / INFERRED / UNKNOWN.
2. Router, match the target type to the cheapest tool that can answer *this* question. Asar slice, `go version -m`, jadx… not Ghidra by default.
3. Escalate last, decompile / GhidraMCP only when strings + metadata can’t settle the goal.

Same permission boundary as always. Different spend curve: stop when the goal has evidence, not when the binary is “fully understood.” If you’ve watched REA-style runs chew context on a feature that lived in one string xref… this is the short path.

→ [https://t.co/2eERuePdR3] · bring a target you’re allowed to inspect.

For the Nerds on how I built this bot and why:

Ghidra is the @NSACyber's open-source reverse-engineering suite—its particular strength is deep native analysis when shell triage isn’t enough: real decompilation, cross-references, call graphs, and type recovery across a whole program, which Reverse Lab reaches last via GhidraMCP so you only pay that cost when strings and metadata can’t answer the goal. Upstream of that, the methodology is adapted from leanrea (@aicodeking)—a CLI-first triage/router approach that batches cheap inventory (file, strings, imports, capped slices) and routes by target type instead of dumping everything into a heavy REA-style session, so you spend tokens on evidence for this question, not on fully understanding the binary.

If you want to use Reverse Engineer Anything  (REA) ....which burns a lot more tokens than leanrea, I have a bot for that too, that sets up a full Clean Room for you. Better have an ULTRA plan for that one;

https://t.co/2PIdOh5uuv

Tons more AI, RE, cyber, N8N, and other grokbot templates here:  https://t.co/383yRBGfAA

But here's what most people get wrong:

Having 20 agents doesn't mean you have a working AI company.

You need a system:
→ 1 coordinator to break down objectives
→ Specialist agents to execute tasks in parallel
→ Shared handoffs so work doesn't restart from zero
→ Independent verification before results are accepted
→ Clear stopping rules to prevent endless retry loops

That's how you turn a folder full of bots into an actual AI workforce.
The repositories are free. Running them may still require an AI subscription, API usage, integrations, or hosting.
Start with one workflow. Make it work. Then scale.

Bookmark this before you waste another week building something that already exists.

→ DISCOVERY: monitor new Solana pools and save the original transaction behind every candidate
→ SCREENING: remove tokens with open mint permissions, concentrated ownership, bundled buying, or weak liquidity
→ ANALYSIS: score the survivors against the same entry checklist instead of inventing a new reason for every coin
→ POSITION SIZE: calculate the order from current equity and the maximum permitted loss
→ EXECUTION: check the obtainable price, submit the order, and confirm what actually filled
→ EXITS: attach the exit conditions and record every partial sale, fee, and remaining position

→ a volume spike produced by the same small group of wallets

→ a missing contract check that stayed unresolved
